<a id="add-project-parameter"></a>

### Add project parameter

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-13 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** add a new project parameter to these categories.

Creates a shared parameter and binds it to one or more categories as a project parameter - "add a parameter called AJ_Status to duct accessories". Every other parameter fragment here writes VALUES into a parameter that already exists; this one makes the parameter. **It is ADMIN risk, not MODIFY, and the reason is worth stating.** A binding changes the project's data structure for everybody who opens the file, it is the thing a client's BIM execution plan governs, and un-binding a parameter discards every value anybody typed into it. That is a different class of change from moving a duct. **The shared parameter file is asked for and never invented.** The earlier library fell back to creating one under a temporary folder when the application had none set. A shared parameter written to a path nobody knows about is a parameter that cannot be re-used on the next project or matched by a colleague - which defeats the whole point of it being SHARED. So the path comes from the request. A path with no file, or a name the file does not hold, is refused (version 3): `createMissing` true makes a new parameter in a file that is there, `createFile` true makes a new file. What either one writes to disk, Undo does not take back. **Re-running it does not make a second parameter.** An existing definition of that name in that group is reused, and an existing binding is extended rather than replaced. Replacing a binding is how a category quietly loses a parameter it had. **The parameter is filed under Data.** The group only decides where it appears in the properties palette, it can be changed in Revit's own Project Parameters dialog afterwards, and asking a modeller for an internal group name buys nothing. **VERSION 2 PUTS REVIT'S SHARED PARAMETER FILE SETTING BACK, AND NAMES A CATEGORY IT COULD NOT BIND** (FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-317). Version 1 pointed Revit at the requested file and left it there. That setting belongs to the Revit session, not to the project: no transaction holds it, so Undo cannot reverse it, and Manage > Shared Parameters stayed pointed at Heron's path in every project afterwards. The setting in force is now read first and put back whatever happens, and `sharedParameterFileRestored` says whether it reads as it did before. And version 1 reported only the categories that came back bound, so a category Revit will not let a project parameter onto simply went missing from the answer. Each one is now checked before it is added, every category asked for is looked for in the binding afterwards, and any that is not there is in `categoriesNotBound` with the reason. If none of them can carry a parameter, nothing is done and the shared parameter file setting is never touched. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="assign-location-data"></a>

### Assign location data

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-24 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** write where each element is onto its own parameters.

Writes where each element actually IS onto its own parameters - the name and the number of the room or space it sits in, each into a parameter of its own, and its level. The *"fill in the location columns"* job that a handover register or a client's asset list needs, and that nothing in Revit fills for you. **IT IS NOT `WRITE_ELEMENT_PARAMETERS`, because the value is not given - it is WORKED OUT.** That fragment writes a value somebody supplies. This one reads each element's position from geometry and derives what to write, per element. Nobody can hand in four hundred different room names. **ROOM AND SPACE ARE NOT THE SAME THING, AND THIS IS THE SINGLE MOST COMMON WAY A LOCATION REGISTER COMES OUT WRONG.** Architecture puts people in ROOMS; MEP calculates in SPACES. A model can hold both, in the same place, with different names and different numbers. Which one is used is asked for, and the report says which was used. Rooms in a LINKED model are asked only with `includeLinks` (D-59), and this model's own room or space wins where both hold an element. **THE STOREY IS CHECKED.** A room on Level 1 lies under a damper on Level 3 in plan; it is taken only when the element is inside it, or above it but still on its storey. Anything else - another floor, below the floor, two rooms equally good - is left unwritten and named with the reason, never written with another floor's name. **THE PROBE POINT IS NUDGED TO THE ROOM'S OWN MID-HEIGHT, and without that the answer is wrong for exactly the elements most often asked about.** The room test needs a point inside the room's VOLUME. A ceiling-mounted diffuser sits above the room's upper limit and tests false from its own position - so a register built the obvious way has every terminal blank. **THE TARGET PARAMETERS MUST ALREADY EXIST.** This fills them; it does not create them. Anything missing is counted and named per parameter, so *"0 written"* is never mysterious. **A TARGET NAME TWO PARAMETERS SHARE IS NOT FILLED.** A shared or project parameter can be bound beside a built-in one of the same name, and Revit's lookup by name then returns one of them at random, in Autodesk's own words - so the room name would land in a field no schedule reads. Counted and named per parameter in `refused`, and neither is touched (D-54 s3, FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-203). This is version 3; the proof below is version 2's, kept as a record, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="copy-parameter-value"></a>

### Copy parameter value

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** copy one parameter's value into another parameter on the same elements.

Copies the value of one parameter into another, on each element. Getting a system name into a shared parameter a schedule can use, filling a client's required field from one Revit already holds, populating a COBie field before handover. **Both parameters must hold the same KIND of value.** A number into a text field is a silent reformat; text into a number is a refusal. The storage types are compared before anything is written and a mismatch stops the whole batch — one wrong-typed pair discovered halfway leaves a set that is half converted with no record of where. **It copies what is STORED, not what is displayed.** A length displayed as "2400 mm" is stored as feet, and copying the displayed string into a text field puts a unit-suffixed string somewhere that a later calculation cannot use. Same storage type means the same internal value moves. **A name two parameters share is neither copied from nor copied into.** A shared or project parameter can be bound beside a built-in one of the same name, and Revit's lookup by name then returns one of them at random, in Autodesk's own words. Either side matching twice puts the element in `ambiguous`, untouched (D-54 s3, FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-203). This is version 2; version 1's proof no longer describes the code and is kept as a record, and the fragment is DRAFT until it is proved again. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="create-global-parameter"></a>

### Create global parameter

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** make a new global parameter for this project.

Creates a global parameter - the single project-wide value that can then be labelled onto dimensions and element parameters to drive them. **THE LIBRARY NAMED THIS GAP ITSELF, AND THAT IS WHY IT EXISTS.** SET_GLOBAL_PARAMETER's own routing table says *"make a global parameter -> NOT HERE"* and routes it to nothing. REPORT_GLOBAL_PARAMETERS lists them, SET_GLOBAL_PARAMETER writes into one that already exists, and until this fragment nothing could make one. A fragment that names its own boundary is the best gap detector in this repository; this is that boundary answered. **IT MAKES THE PARAMETER AND DOES NOT SET ITS VALUE.** The new global holds whatever its spec starts at, and writing a value is SET_GLOBAL_PARAMETER's job. That split is the same one ADD_PROJECT_PARAMETER and WRITE_ELEMENT_PARAMETERS already keep: making the thing and filling it in are different operations with different risks, and folding them together would mean a typo in a value silently created a parameter as well. **IT IS ADMIN AND SET_GLOBAL_PARAMETER IS MODIFY, WHICH IS NOT A CLAIM THAT THIS ONE IS MORE DANGEROUS.** Setting a global re-drives every dimension labelled by it and can move walls on twelve levels; this creates a value nothing is labelled by yet and moves nothing at all. The levels differ because the CLASS of change differs - this changes what the project CONTAINS for everybody who opens it, which is the thing a BIM execution plan governs, where setting changes what the model LOOKS LIKE. That is the same reading ADD_PROJECT_PARAMETER applies to itself. **RE-RUNNING IT DOES NOT MAKE A SECOND ONE.** An existing global of that name is handed back rather than duplicated, and the findings say so plainly. Revit refuses duplicate global names outright, so the alternative to checking is a throw in the middle of somebody's transaction. **A FAMILY DOCUMENT CANNOT HAVE GLOBAL PARAMETERS AT ALL**, and that is reported as *this kind of document cannot* rather than as a failure to create. The two read identically to a tool and completely differently to a person. **WHAT IS REPORTED IS WHAT THE PROJECT HOLDS AFTERWARDS**, read back by name after the write rather than assumed from the call returning. That is the rule this project exists around. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="edit-text-values"></a>

### Edit text values

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-24 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** change the text that is already there rather than replacing it - a prefix, a suffix or a find and replace in a parameter, a text note or a name, renaming plans and other views, sheets, schedules, templates and types.

Transforms text that is already on each element - add a prefix, add a suffix, or replace part of it - instead of overwriting it with one flat value. A text note's own wording is one more field: find and replace across text notes, or set a note's whole wording. So is an element's own NAME: plans and other views, sheets, schedules, templates and types are renamed here, by replacing part of the name. **A TEXT NOTE'S WORDING IS FIELD "Text"** (version 3, 2026-10-12, the gap fill). It is no parameter - it is the note's own text - so it is read and written through the note itself, and compared without the closing carriage return Revit adds. Mode "set" writes the whole wording, and only there: one value on a parameter is WRITE_ELEMENT_PARAMETERS. **`WRITE_ELEMENT_PARAMETERS` SETS A LITERAL AND THAT IS A DIFFERENT JOB.** *"Put AJ- in front of every mark"* cannot be done by setting a value, because the value is different on every element. This one reads first, transforms, and writes back. **THE ELEMENT'S OWN NAME IS JUST ANOTHER FIELD**, and treating it as one is the decision this fragment makes. The earlier library had a rename fragment and a prefix/suffix fragment carrying the same four transformations twice. `field: "Name"` edits `Element.Name`; anything else is a parameter. One mechanism, so a fix to the replace rule cannot reach one of them and miss the other. **AN ELEMENT WHOSE TEXT DOES NOT CONTAIN THE SEARCH TERM IS `untouched`, NOT A FAILURE.** Running a replace across a mixed set and having half of it not match is the normal case. Counting those as errors makes the report unusable; counting them as successes reports work that did not happen. **IT READS BACK.** Every element it says it changed was re-read after the write, and anything Revit accepted and then altered is reported separately. A count of attempts is not a count of changes. **NOTHING IS DONE TO AN EMPTY VALUE.** A prefix on a blank parameter would create a value where the modeller had none, which is a different edit from the one asked for and would look like data. **A FIELD NAME TWO PARAMETERS SHARE IS NOT EDITED.** A shared or project parameter can be bound beside a built-in one of the same name, and Revit's lookup by name then returns one of them at random, in Autodesk's own words. Such an element goes in `ambiguous`, untouched (D-54 s3, FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-203). **RE-RUNNING IT MUST NOT STACK, AND A TYPE IS EDITED ONCE** (version 6, when EDIT_PARAMETER_TEXT was merged in). A prefix or suffix already on the value is not added again, so a second run leaves `AJ_M-01` rather than `AJ_AJ_M-01`. A field that lives on the TYPE - Type Mark, Manufacturer, Model - is written once however many of its instances are handed in, and the types changed are named in `typesEdited`, because every other instance of them changed too. **A RENAME IS CHECKED WHOLE BEFORE ONE NAME IS WRITTEN** (version 7, when RENAME_ELEMENTS was merged in). With field Name - a view, a sheet, a schedule, a template or a type renamed by replacing part of its name - every new name is worked out first and checked against the others in the batch and against the names already in the model. Two the same, or one already taken, and NOTHING is renamed: `collisions` says which, because a batch half renamed carries two conventions. Renaming a TYPE renames it everywhere it is used. `notMatched` names the elements a replace found nothing to replace in. **FIELD "Family" RENAMES THE LOADED FAMILY** (version 8, when RENAME_FAMILY was merged in) - the component itself, one level above the type name, from an instance, a type or the family handed in. Every type in it and every instance follows, across the model, and the answer counts them. One family per call, never an in-place one; mode set gives the whole new name, and prefix, suffix and replace work as on any field. A name another family holds is refused before anything is renamed. The .rfa on disk keeps its own name.

<a id="export-parameters-to-csv"></a>

### Export parameters to CSV

**DRAFT - not yet usable in a chat - refused until proved (D-117).**

**What it does:** get these parameters out into a spreadsheet.

Writes chosen parameters of a set of elements to a CSV file - one row per element, the element id always first - so the values can be edited in a spreadsheet and brought back. **THE ELEMENT ID IS THE FIRST COLUMN AND IT IS NOT OPTIONAL.** A round trip needs a key: without one, an edited file cannot be matched back to the elements it came from except by a name that may not be unique and may itself have been what somebody edited. **Values are written the way Revit DISPLAYS them, not the way it stores them.** A length goes out as the millimetres somebody recognises rather than as decimal feet. That is what makes the file editable by a human - and it is the same convention anything reading the file back has to use, or the numbers change meaning on the way home. **Fields containing a comma, a quote or a line break are quoted properly.** A Comments field with a comma in it silently splits a row into two columns otherwise, and every column after it is wrong for that element only - which is the hardest kind of error to see in a spreadsheet. **It writes a file, which is why it is PUBLISH.** The model is untouched; a file appears somewhere other people can open, and the path is reported because somebody has to be told where. **A parameter an element does not carry is written as empty, not skipped.** Every row has the same columns, or the file is not a table.

<a id="read-element-parameters"></a>

### Read element parameters

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-24 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** reads one named parameter off every element.

Reads one named parameter off every element, and says which of three things was true for each: it had a value, it had the parameter but blank, or it did not have the parameter at all. **VERSION 2 FIXED TWO WAYS THIS SAID `absent` WHILE THE VALUE WAS RIGHT THERE.** Version 1 asked `LookupParameter` and nothing else, which is correct for an instance parameter and wrong for most of what gets asked: | Asked for | v1 answered | Why it was wrong | |---|---|---| | A **type** parameter - size, fire rating, manufacturer | `absent`, every element | Most schedule columns live once on the type, not per instance | | **"Level"** on walls or ducts | `absent` for both | A wall has no level-named parameter at all; a duct calls it "Reference Level" | The second is the dangerous one. Across a mixed set, air terminals answered and walls and ducts did not, so the report read *"most of this model has no level"* - which is not a thing that can be true, and looks like a modelling problem rather than a reading one. The type is now asked **second**, never first, so an instance parameter of the same name still wins - that is the one the modeller edited. `resolvedFrom` records which answered, because *"they share one value"* and *"they each carry the same value"* are different findings with different fixes. **THE ANSWER IS SAID IN WORDS** (version 5). `values` and `resolvedFrom` are dictionaries, and a dictionary reached a chat as its count alone: one parameter read on four connectors answered *"values 4 entry(ies)"* and not one value (Revit 2020, 2026-10-22). The add-in now sends a dictionary's first entries beside its count; `findings` is the same answer in this card's own words - *"Allow Slope Adjustments": 4 of 4 carry a value, 0 blank, 0 absent. 14194: Yes (instance); 7492: Yes (instance); ...* - every element read (version 6), then the blank and the absent ids. It is one string, so no cut on the way to a chat can shorten it to a number. **LEVEL IS THE ONLY SPECIAL CASE.** Category, Family and Type are how a table is labelled rather than something read off an element, and D-20 keeps that at the edge where the user is. **"Text" on a text note is what the note says** (version 3): its wording, with each paragraph's list type - and (version 4) whether it is a numbered or bulleted list and which paragraphs are bold, italic or underlined.

<a id="read-element-table"></a>

### Read element table

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-07 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** these elements and the named parameters, as rows the Companion can edit.

Reads the named parameters of the given elements into ONE table, for the Heron Companion page (D-108, docs/40 section 8.2): one row per element - its id, UniqueId, category, family and type - and for each parameter the value as the modeller sees it, and whether that cell can be edited, with the reason when it cannot. **It is the table a chat opens with revit_edit_table, and the chat is told only how many rows it holds.** The rows go to the page; that is what keeps a schedule of ninety units from costing the chat ninety rows of tokens. **Why one string.** A fragment's list output reaches the caller as its first three names (FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-195), and a table needs every row. So the table crosses as one JSON string, `tableJson`, format 1 - the workaround report-category-overrides already uses - until a central reply fix lands. **Editable means an INSTANCE parameter this element carries once**, which is not read-only and holds text, a number or a Yes/No. A TYPE parameter is shown and marked not editable here: changing it changes every element of that type, which is a different question from editing a row. A name two parameters share is marked not editable, never guessed between (D-54 s3, FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-203). An element reference cannot be typed as text. **Values are read the way read-element-parameters reads them**: the display string first, in the project's own units, then the raw text. That display string is also what the write half compares against before it writes anything (set-parameter-values-by-id, Article 12c). Caps at maxRows rows (2,000 when not given) and says so in `truncated`.

<a id="renumber-sequential"></a>

### Renumber sequential

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-14 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** number these elements one after another, in the order given.

Writes a RUNNING SEQUENCE into one parameter, across a batch, in the order the elements arrive - D-1, D-2, D-3 along a corridor. **Writing ONE value onto one element is WRITE_ELEMENT_PARAMETERS, not this.** The sequence is what makes this a separate job. See the routing table below, which is kept in a comment for a reason worth knowing before editing it. **It does not decide the ORDER, and that is the most important thing about it.** Numbering left to right, along a corridor, clockwise round a core or simply in selection order are different jobs with different right answers, and a fragment that picked one would be silently wrong for the rest. The caller hands the elements in the order it wants them numbered - D-33: never assume an input. **It checks for collisions BEFORE writing anything.** Revit will happily give two doors the same number and say nothing; the drawing then looks finished and is wrong. Every intended value is compared against what the rest of the model already holds, and a clash stops the whole batch rather than producing a half-renumbered set nobody can unpick. **A NAME TWO PARAMETERS SHARE GETS NO NUMBER.** A shared or project parameter can be bound beside a built-in one of the same name, and Revit's lookup by name then returns one of them at random, in Autodesk's own words - so a number would land in a field no tag reads. Those elements are reported in `ambiguous` and skipped before any number is given out, so the sequence has no gap (D-54 s3, FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-203). ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

<a id="report-global-parameters"></a>

### Report global parameters

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-09-07 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** list the global parameters and what each one drives.

Lists every GLOBAL parameter in the project - its value, whether a formula drives it, whether it only reports, and WHICH DIMENSIONS IT DRIVES. Read-only. **A GLOBAL PARAMETER IS NOT A PROJECT PARAMETER, AND MIXING THEM UP WASTES A SESSION.** A project parameter is a COLUMN: every door carries its own value. A global parameter is ONE VALUE for the whole model, attachable to dimensions and to element parameters, so changing it MOVES GEOMETRY. *"Corridor width = 1800"* as one number that eight dimensions obey is a global parameter. **THE INTERESTING PART IS WHAT IT DRIVES, NOT ITS VALUE.** The value is one number. The list of DIMENSIONS labelled by it is the list of things that move when somebody edits that number - and it is the only answer to *"why did that wall shift when I changed a figure in a dialog"*. Without this fragment a model driven by globals looks, from here, like a model where things move for no reason. **NOT EVERY DOCUMENT ALLOWS THEM.** A family document does not, and neither do some template states. That is asked first and said plainly, because an empty list otherwise reads as *"this model has none"* when the truth is *"this kind of document cannot have any"* - two different answers that look identical. **Creating or setting one is deliberately not here.** Setting a global parameter moves geometry, which makes it a MODIFY job and not a report, and the create call changed shape at Revit 2022. **SETTING ONE IS NOW `SET_GLOBAL_PARAMETER`**, built 2026-09-06. That sentence above said where it did NOT belong and nothing said where it DID, so for a while nothing in the library could write a global at all - and `WRITE_ELEMENT_PARAMETERS` cannot stand in, because a global's value is not a parameter on an element. Read this fragment's `drives` list before writing: it is exactly what will move. Creating one is `CREATE_GLOBAL_PARAMETER`, written 2026-09-07 - not here, but no longer nowhere. **Neither can RUN yet:** the executor has only `run_fragment_read`, so nothing that writes can be executed as a fragment at all, whatever its risk says.

<a id="report-parameter-inventory"></a>

### Report parameter inventory

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-10-18 (Revit 2020).

**What it does:** every parameter this element actually has, before you know any of their names.

Lists every parameter an element ACTUALLY carries - name, storage type, instance or type, whether it is built-in or shared, read-only or not, and its current value. The discovery step before any bulk read or write. It changes nothing. **IT ANSWERS THE QUESTION YOU HAVE BEFORE YOU KNOW THE NAMES.** `READ_ELEMENT_PARAMETERS` reads a parameter you can already name. This one answers *"what parameters does this duct even have"* - and the two get asked in that order. Guessing a plausible name and finding it absent is the commonest wasted round trip in this whole library, and it is avoidable by looking first. IT EXISTS BECAUSE THE QUESTION WAS GOING TO `REPORT_GLOBAL_PARAMETERS`. Measured before this batch, both *"list every parameter that exists on this element"* and *"what parameters can I filter on"* resolved there. **A global parameter is one value for the whole model**; this is the list of columns on one element. That fragment's own purpose already says they get mixed up and that mixing them up wastes a session. **THE PARAMETER GROUP IS DELIBERATELY NOT REPORTED**, and the reason is worth keeping: `Definition.ParameterGroup` is gone by Revit 2027 and its replacement `GetGroupTypeId` has never existed on 2020. Neither works at both ends, and every fragment here is one implementation for all eight releases. The group is a sorting convenience in a dialog; nothing about reading or writing a value needs it. **THREE KINDS, AND ONLY THREE CAN HONESTLY BE TOLD APART.** Built-in, Shared, and *"project or family - not shared"*. Revit's API carries no flag separating a parameter defined inside the Family Editor from one added through Project Parameters once both are on an element. Reporting a guess as a fact is worse than reporting the bucket, so the third is named as the bucket it is. **SAMPLING ONE ELEMENT IS THE DEFAULT AND THE UNION IS THE OPTION.** One element answers the question fast and is representative of its type. A mixed set of different families genuinely varies, and `sampleOnly` off is how that variation is found - at the cost of reading everything. **VERSION 2: EACH PARAMETER WITH ITS GUID, AND THE FULL RECORD.** Two parameters sharing a name are both listed, and sameNameTwice names them; fullRecord gives the whole record as one string. See the note above the contract.

A tag or schedule built on the file's parameter does not read either. **IT NEVER CHANGES THE SETTING, THE FILE OR THE MODEL.** Run it before adding shared parameters to a family or a project.

<a id="set-global-parameter"></a>

### Set global parameter

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** change the global parameter that drives the model.

Writes a new value into a global parameter - the single project-wide value that drives dimensions and element parameters wherever it is labelled. **THIS MOVES GEOMETRY, AND THAT IS WHY IT IS ITS OWN FRAGMENT.** REPORT_GLOBAL_PARAMETERS lists them and says outright that setting one is not a report's job. It is right: changing a global re-drives every dimension labelled by it, so a one-line edit can move walls on twelve levels. Nothing else in this library could do it, and nothing else should. **A GLOBAL'S VALUE IS NOT A PARAMETER ON AN ELEMENT, WHICH IS WHY WRITE_ELEMENT_PARAMETERS CANNOT REACH IT.** A global parameter IS an element, but its value is read and written through its own pair of calls rather than through the parameter collection every other fragment uses. Pointing the ordinary parameter writer at one finds nothing to write. **THE VALUE ARRIVES ALREADY BUILT, AND THAT IS DELIBERATE.** A global holds a length, a number, a string or an element id, and the value handed in carries its own type - the same choice OVERRIDE_GRAPHICS_IN_VIEW makes with its settings object, and for the same reason: it keeps one implementation working on eight releases without a units API anywhere near it. A length arrives in Revit's internal feet, converted at the edge (D-20). **TWO KINDS OF GLOBAL CANNOT BE SET AT ALL, AND BOTH LOOK ORDINARY.** One driven by a FORMULA takes its value from the formula, so a write is refused. A REPORTING one reads a dimension out of the model - it is an output, not an input, and it can never be written. Both are checked before anything is attempted, and both come back as a named reason rather than as a failure. **A TYPE MISMATCH IS REFUSED RATHER THAN COERCED.** Writing text into a length is not a conversion anybody meant, and Revit's own answer to it is not consistent enough to rely on. **THE VALUE IS READ BACK AFTER WRITING.** A global that refuses can return without raising, and the whole point of the fragment is what moved - so what is reported is what the model holds afterwards, not what was asked for. **A FAMILY DOCUMENT CANNOT HAVE GLOBAL PARAMETERS AT ALL**, and an empty list there means *this kind of document cannot*, not *there are none*. Asked in one, this says so instead of reporting a missing parameter. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16).

| **You get** | changed, after, findings |

<a id="set-parameter-values-by-id"></a>

### Set parameter values by ID

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-24 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** a different value for each named element, only if nothing moved since it was read.

Writes a DIFFERENT value into a named instance parameter on each of several elements, each element named by its id and UniqueId - the write half of the Heron Companion's editable table (D-108, docs/40 section 8.4). Every row carries the value the table SHOWED, and nothing is written unless every row still holds exactly that. **All or nothing, before anything is written (Article 12c, Golden Rule 21).** The first pass only checks: the element is still there and is the same element, the parameter is there once, it is not read-only, and it still holds the value the table showed. One row failing any of that and the whole run changes NOTHING and says which rows and why - the owner's choice on 2026-09-29, question 2 of docs/40 section 18. The page shows them and the modeller presses Apply again. **The elements come from the rows, never from the selection.** Applied minutes after the table was read, a fragment that took the selection would write onto whatever is selected then. So there is no `elements` input. **Values are written the way write-element-parameters writes them**: text as text; a number through SetValueString, in the document's own units, so "300 mm" and "300" mean what the modeller sees; a Yes/No as 1 or 0 from Yes, No, True, False, On, Off, 1 or 0. After ONE regeneration every row is read back and `resultJson` carries what Revit now holds, not what was asked. **Rows cross as text**: `id|uniqueId|parameter|was|new`, each field percent-encoded so a value may hold a bar or a semicolon, rows separated by semicolons. **Or by a value each element holds** (version 2): a first row of the key parameter and the categories to look in, then rows of a key value and the values to write. A key matching no element, or more than one, is refused for that row alone; the other rows are written and read back. A key with a * is a pattern (version 8): it names every element or type whose key matches, and the same values go onto all of them - that row written whole or not at all. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one - the operation's TransactionGroup makes the whole Apply one entry in Revit's undo list (Golden Rule 16). **Or from a spreadsheet** (version 7, when IMPORT_PARAMETER_VALUES was merged in): `csvPath` names a CSV whose first column is each element's id and whose other columns are parameter names - a different value per element, from a table edited outside Revit, the client's equipment tags sent back. Each cell is an id row, so all or nothing holds for the file: an id naming no element here, a missing parameter or a value Revit will not take, and nothing is written. `blankCells` - skip or clear - says what an empty cell means; it is asked, never assumed. The rows alone name the elements, as for every row.

<a id="transfer-project-parameters-between-documents"></a>

### Transfer project parameters between documents

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-02 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** bring the project parameters over from the other project.

Binds this project the same shared parameters another OPEN project has - *"bring the project parameters over from the template"*, *"set up the same parameters as last job"*. **IT IS ADMIN RISK, NOT MODIFY, for the reason [ADD_PROJECT_PARAMETER](../../../brain/fragments/add-project-parameter/fragment.yaml) already states**: a binding changes the project's data structure for everybody who opens the file, it is what a client's BIM execution plan governs, and un-binding a parameter discards every value anybody typed into it. Doing it for a dozen parameters at once does not make it smaller. **THE SHARED PARAMETER FILE IS REQUIRED, AND THAT IS NOT THIS FRAGMENT BEING AWKWARD.** A shared parameter's definition lives in the .txt file, not in the project. The source document knows the parameter's name, its GUID and what it is bound to; it does not hold the definition needed to bind it somewhere else. So each parameter is matched **by GUID** in the file you name - a name match would happily bind a different parameter that happens to share a word. **A NON-SHARED PROJECT PARAMETER CANNOT BE CARRIED AT ALL, and it is named rather than skipped silently.** A project parameter created without a shared definition exists only inside its own file; the API cannot recreate one elsewhere. Those come back in `skipped` saying so, because a transfer that quietly leaves out three of ten parameters is worse than one that refuses. **AN EXISTING BINDING IS NEVER REPLACED.** Re-binding is how a category quietly loses a parameter it had, along with every value in it. A parameter already bound here goes to `clashed` and this project is left alone - including when the source binds it to more categories than this project does. **THE PARAMETER GROUP IS CARRIED WHERE IT CAN BE READ, AND THE FALLBACK IS REPORTED.** `Definition.ParameterGroup` is gone by Revit 2027 and `GetGroupTypeId` has never existed on 2020 - a matched pair where neither spelling works at both ends. Both are tried at run time; where neither answers, the parameter is filed under **Data** and named in `regrouped`, so a parameter that landed in a different part of the properties palette is something you are told rather than something you find. **BOTH PROJECTS MUST BE OPEN IN THE SAME REVIT.** The source is found by its title among the open documents; if it is not open, the open ones are listed and nothing is attempted. Linked documents are not offered. **VERSION 2 PUTS REVIT'S SHARED PARAMETER FILE SETTING BACK** (FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-317). Version 1 pointed Revit at the file asked for and left it there. That setting belongs to the Revit session, not to either project: no transaction holds it, so Undo cannot reverse it, and Manage > Shared Parameters stayed pointed at that path afterwards. The setting in force is now read first and put back once the bindings are made, whatever happened, and `sharedParameterFileRestored` says whether it reads as it did before. If it cannot be read first, nothing is attempted; if it cannot be put back, `refused` says so and names both paths. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one (Golden Rule 16). **The undo belongs to THIS document** - the source project is only read.

<a id="write-element-parameters"></a>

### Write element parameters

**Usable in a chat.** Proved on a real model on 2026-11-16 (Revit 2024).

**What it does:** write one parameter value onto these elements.

Writes one named parameter on many elements, and reports every element it did NOT write and why - read-only, absent, a name two of its parameters share, or a kind this fragment refuses. It is the write half of FRG-PAR-001's read, and it takes the value as TEXT on purpose. A number alone cannot be written safely: Revit stores lengths in decimal feet, and the same fragment is asked to set an airflow, an area and a comment. See the implementation note - this is the decision most likely to be "improved" by somebody who has not hit it. **It reports what the MODEL holds, not what was asked for.** Revit accepts a size and then snaps it to the nearest size its type allows - the set returns TRUE, nothing throws, and a pipe asked for 77 comes out 80. Version 1 trusted that return value and would have reported a clean success over a different number. `snapped` is that case, named and carrying ids. **Version 3 refuses a name that two parameters share.** A shared or project parameter can be bound beside a built-in one of the same name, and a curtain wall type carries its grid and mullion settings once for each direction. Revit's lookup by name then returns one of them - at random, in Autodesk's own words - and the read-back, looking the name up the same way, would have confirmed whichever it was. Such an element is reported in `ambiguous` and nothing on it is touched (D-54 s3, FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-203). **Version 4 writes a Yes/No parameter.** Revit keeps a tick box as the number 1 or 0, so version 3 sent it through `SetValueString`, which returned false for it: one tick box on 15 units was refused all 15 times with `No`, and again with `0` (FRAGMENT-ISSUES 5b-247). It now finds a Yes/No parameter first, on every release from 2020, and takes Yes/No, True/False, On/Off, 1/0 and Ticked/Unticked in any case - anything else is refused and `findings` names the value and those words. The read-back is unchanged: `AsInteger` after the regeneration must equal what was asked. An element already holding the value is left alone and counted in `alreadyThat`, so a second run changes nothing and says so. Text, numbers and element references go exactly the way they went in version 3; `alreadyThat` is filled for a tick box only. **Version 5 takes a material, a level or a family type by name.** **Version 6 clears a parameter back to EMPTY** - `clear` true, the value left empty - when REMOVE_PARAMETER_VALUE was merged in. An empty parameter and a zero are not the same thing, so a clear is Revit's own, on every storage kind, and never a 0 written. A text built-in Revit will not clear takes the empty string instead; a type parameter reached from instances is refused, because clearing it empties every other instance too; one already empty is `alreadyEmpty`, and every clear is read back. ASSUMES AN OPEN TRANSACTION and does not open one. Golden Rule 16 puts the TransactionGroup at the OPERATION, so that one user action is one undo; a fragment that opened its own would add a second entry to the undo stack and break exactly the rule it looks like it is obeying.

| | |
|---|---|
| **Kind** | Changes the model (`MODIFY`) |
| **Reached by** | asking in a Claude chat |
| **Works on** | what is selected in Revit: elements |
| **You say** | **parameter name** - text<br>**value** - text<br>**clear** - yes or no - true or false; optional |
| **You get** | written, snapped, cleared |
| **Built for Revit** | 2020, 2021, 2022, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026, 2027 |
| **Proved on Revit** | 2024 |
| **Capability** | `WRITE_ELEMENT_PARAMETERS` |

**How to use it**

1. Open the model in Revit and connect Heron: press **Heron** on the Heron tab, so its heron turns orange.
2. Select what it works on in Revit (elements) - or name it in the same request, and Heron finds it first.
3. Turn **Changes** on in Heron's **Settings** (Heron tab).
4. In a Claude chat, ask in your own words, for example *"set the comments on these"*. Say the values under **You say** in the same sentence.
5. Heron makes the change as **one entry in Revit's Undo list**. With **Ask to Keep** on, Revit asks **Keep or Discard** first; Ctrl+Z takes it back.

Other ways to ask: *"set the comments to X"* · *"write the airflow back"*
